Both [S2] and [S3] describe sparse coding as a generalization of VQ where signals are represented by linear combinations of dictionary atoms, allowing 'more than one nonzero entry' and 'arbitrary values' for coefficients. Furthermore, both sources state that learned dictionaries (the method implied) 'deliver increased flexibility and the ability to adapt to specific signal data'. All factual components of the claim are present in the provided evidence.

The method is closely related to Fractal Compression, which also works on block entities but relies on self-similarity and affine transformations [S2][S3].

The claim states that the method (Sparse Representation/Sparse Coding) is closely related to Fractal Compression, works on block entities, and relies on self-similarity and affine transformations. The evidence in Source [S2] and Source [S3] explicitly discusses 'Fractal Compression' in a dedicated section. It states that Fractal Compression 'relies on the fact that some parts of the dataset (volume) often resemble other parts (self-similarity)' and that 'Similar to vector quantization, the idea of fractal compression is to work on block entities'. Furthermore, the passage in Source [S3] mentions that fractal compression 'stores per data block the position of another different-sized data block of the same volume and additionally stores the affine [transformations]'. While the text distinguishes between the two methods (Sparse Coding vs. Fractal Compression), it confirms that Fractal Compression indeed works on block entities and relies on self-similarity and affine transformations, which are the specific facts cited in the claim regarding Fractal Compression.

The concept of dictionary-based sparse representation is a generalization of Vector Quantization (VQ) [S2][S3].

This directly supports the claim that dictionary-based sparse representation is a generalization of Vector Quantization.
